chapter: Style, peers and the 1963 New Orleans scene
title: Henry Red Allen's imitation of Armstrong and why he did not rise
summary: Watts and Alfred agree Red Allen was a fine player but copied Louis too closely, which they believe limited his reputation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, yeah. And don't forget my little teacher now, Henry Red Allen.
He sees specs, too, and he blow.
But let me tell you why he didn't make much of a reputation, what I heard, from musicians, you know.
He said he tried to imitate Lewis too much. Well, he did. You see, that's why he didn't make a reputation like Lewis.
He didn't try to work in a style of his own, you see.

So that's what one of the musicians... Too much repetition. Yeah, that's what one of the boys come out there with Duke, you see. Yeah, yeah. He told me, I said, how come Alan ain't got on the top like Lewis? He said, well, he imitated Lewis. Yeah, yeah. He said he should have a style of his own. Then he said he played nice trumpet, playing the trumpet. Oh, yeah.
But he said he imitated. Too much.
